blocks.orig: Going on safari in Africa is an experience that you certainly won’t ever forget, and epic safari photography makes sure that you are able to share the incredible experience with family and friends. In fact, the photos that you take while on safari are one of the best ways to share this experience with the ones you love.  For that reason, you will want to make sure you are able to take the best pictures you possibly can.
blocks.html: An African safari is something you certainly won’t forget, and strong safari photography lets you pass that incredible experience on to family and friends. The pictures you take on safari are, in fact, among the best ways to share the trip with the people you love. So it makes sense to do everything you can to come home with the best possible photos.

blocks.orig: Here, travel blogger and photographer Josh from the Wanderlust Travel and Photos Blog delves into some of the best tips and tricks that he has learned during many years of landscape and wildlife photography. “Using these tips, I can assure you that you will be able to capture some very memorable photographs that you will treasure for a lifetime,” says Josh.
blocks.html: In this article, travel blogger and photographer Josh of the Wanderlust Travel and Photos Blog shares some of the most useful tips and tricks he has picked up over many years of photographing landscapes and wildlife. “Follow these tips and I can promise you will come away with some truly memorable photographs to treasure for the rest of your life,” Josh says.

blocks.orig: 1. Safari Photography 101: The Right Camera Equipment
blocks.html: 1. Safari photography basics: the right camera gear

blocks.orig: One of the easiest ways to improve your safari photographs is to make sure you have the right camera equipment with you.  You will be spending quite a bit of time in a vehicle while on safari, and you will be photographing animals outside the vehicle.  This makes photography while on safari very different to other types of photography that you might shoot.
blocks.html: Bringing the right camera equipment is one of the simplest ways to get better safari photographs. On safari you spend a good deal of time inside a vehicle, photographing animals that are outside it. That makes safari photography quite unlike most other kinds of photography you may have tried.

blocks.orig: Having the right equipment with you will keep you more comfortable, keep your camera safe, and allow you to capture more captivating photographs.  If you would like to know more about what types of photography equipment I would recommend bringing on safari, make sure you check out my Safari Photography Guide.
blocks.html: With the right gear you will be more comfortable, your camera will be better protected and your photographs will be more striking. If you want to find out which types of photography equipment I suggest taking on safari, have a look at my Safari Photography Guide.

blocks.orig: 2. Use Shutter Priority With a Fast Shutter Speed
blocks.html: 2. Shoot in shutter priority with a fast shutter speed

blocks.orig: This is a critically important step.  Unless you are planning on shooting a stationary object such as a landscape, you will need to make sure your camera is set to “Shutter Priority” mode.  If your camera doesn’t have a Shutter Priority mode, then you will want to make sure it is set to “Action Shot” or your camera’s equivalent.  Doing this will allow you to free the motion of the animals that you are photographing.  If you don’t adjust this setting, the pictures that you take will wind up blurry.
blocks.html: This step really matters. Unless you intend to photograph something that does not move, such as a landscape, set your camera to “Shutter Priority” mode. If your camera doesn’t offer a Shutter Priority mode, choose “Action Shot” or whatever your camera’s equivalent is called. This lets you freeze the movement of the animals in front of your lens. If you don’t change this setting, your pictures will come out blurry.

blocks.orig: When your camera is set to Shutter Priority mode, you are able to specify which shutter speed you want to use. Then your camera decides which aperture to use to get the best exposure.  If you are unfamiliar with the concepts of shutter speed and aperture, read more in my article on taking pictures in low light situations.
blocks.html: In Shutter Priority mode you choose the shutter speed yourself, and the camera then picks the aperture that gives the best exposure. If shutter speed and aperture are new concepts to you, my article on shooting in low light explains them in more detail.

blocks.orig: Essentially, by adjusting how fast your camera takes the picture (the shutter speed), you are able to freeze the motion of the animals that you are photographing.  Depending on the animal you are shooting and what they are doing, you are going to want to adjust the shutter speed to get the shot.  For instance, if I am shooting a buffalo that is sitting still and grazing, I can safely use a shutter speed between 1/50 and 1/320 of a second and not have any motion blur.  However, if I am shooting a cheetah running, then a much faster shutter speed of 1/1000 to 1/1250 of a second will be necessary.
blocks.html: In short, by changing how quickly the camera takes the picture (the shutter speed) you can freeze the motion of the animals you are photographing. The right shutter speed depends on which animal you are shooting and what it is doing at that moment. Take a buffalo standing still and grazing: here I can comfortably use a shutter speed somewhere between 1/50 and 1/320 of a second without any motion blur. A cheetah at full sprint, on the other hand, calls for a far faster shutter speed of 1/1000 to 1/1250 of a second.

blocks.orig: 3. Use the Rule of Thirds for the Best Safari Photography
blocks.html: 3. Apply the rule of thirds for better safari photographs

blocks.orig: One of the best tips for framing the photographs that you take is to use the Rule of Thirds.  This is a great general photography tip that can be especially useful while on safari photographing wildlife.  Instead of composing all of your shots with the animals in the centre of the frame, try to compose your shots with the animals to either the left or the right of centre.  By following this rule, you will compose shots that are much more interesting to the eye.
blocks.html: When it comes to framing your photographs, one of the most valuable tips is the Rule of Thirds. It is a useful general photography principle that comes into its own when you are photographing wildlife on safari. Rather than placing the animal in the centre of every frame, try composing your shots with the animal to the left or right of centre. Shots composed this way are far more interesting to look at.

blocks.orig: In my example below, I have taken two shots of the same elephant that we encountered while on safari in Lake Manyara National Park in Tanzania. In the shot on the left, I have centred the elephant in the middle of the frame. On the right, I followed the Rule of Thirds and positioned the elephant in the right third of my shot.  Judge for yourself as to which of the two photographs is more visually appealing.
blocks.html: In the example below you can see two photographs of the same elephant, which we came across on safari in Lake Manyara National Park in Tanzania. For the left-hand shot I placed the elephant right in the middle of the frame. For the right-hand one I applied the Rule of Thirds and put the elephant in the right third of the picture. Decide for yourself which of the two is more pleasing to the eye.

blocks.orig: If there is only one tip you take away from this article, then I hope it’s this one!  The cardinal rule for wildlife photography is to always focus on the eyes of the animals that you are photographing.  Instead of just snapping a lot of photographs when you see an animal, wait for the animal to look your way. Then make sure you focus on their eyes.
blocks.html: If you remember just one tip from this article, I hope it’s this. The golden rule of wildlife photography is to focus on the animal's eyes every single time. Rather than firing off lots of frames the moment you spot an animal, wait until it turns towards you. Then make sure the eyes are in focus.

blocks.orig: By focusing on the animal’s eyes, you give the viewer the perception that the animals are looking through the photograph – directly at them.  This will create much more captivating photographs than pictures where the animals are looking away.  This is especially important if you are taking a close-up shot of an animal. This is what I did here with this shot of a lioness in the Serengeti National Park.  It takes some patience, but focusing on the eyes of the animals is the single most effective way to make your safari photographs more memorable.
blocks.html: When the animal’s eyes are sharp, the viewer gets the feeling that the animal is gazing out of the photograph, straight at them. Such pictures are far more compelling than those in which the animal is looking elsewhere, and this matters most of all in a close-up. That is exactly what I did in this shot of a lioness in the Serengeti National Park. It calls for a bit of patience, but focusing on the eyes is the single most effective thing you can do to make your safari photographs more memorable.

blocks.orig: The last safari photography tip that I have for you is to always keep your camera ready while on safari.  You never know what animals will be around the next turn, or what you might see over the next ridge while on safari.  If you don’t have your camera ready, you might miss a wildlife photography shot of a lifetime.  I was only able to capture this cute photo of two dik-diks in the Serengeti looking at me because I had my camera ready when we saw them.  A few seconds later, they were off and running.
blocks.html: My final safari photography tip is simple: keep your camera ready at all times while on safari. You can never tell which animals are waiting around the next bend or what might appear beyond the next ridge. If your camera isn’t ready, the wildlife shot of a lifetime may pass you by. I only managed to capture this charming photo of two dik-diks in the Serengeti looking straight at me because my camera was ready the moment we spotted them. A few seconds later they had bolted.
